why_how.text: Licenses arrive only by mail, so DMV needs your current address.
New residents face two deadlines, and every driver carries the registration card.

scenario.text: Rosa moves to Virginia from another state.

reasoning.text: New Virginians owe a state license within sixty days and title, registration and plates within thirty days.

result.text: Rosa gets her title, registration and plates within thirty days, and her Virginia license within sixty.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking new residents have sixty days for everything.

correction.text: Newcomers owe licenses in sixty days but plates in thirty, front and rear with decals.

prompt.text: Rosa just moved to Virginia. Which is due first, her license or her plates?

answer.text: Her title, registration and plates, within thirty days; the license has sixty.

rationale.text: Newcomers owe plates in thirty days and licenses in sixty.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on registration, insurance and other information. We start with the paperwork that every driver deals with. Virginia licenses arrive only by mail, which is why DMV must know your current address. New residents have two deadlines, one for the license and one for the vehicle's title, registration and plates. And every driver must keep the registration card in the vehicle on every drive, with local registration required in some cities and counties. By the end of this lesson you should know how licenses are delivered, how soon to report a move, and the two newcomer deadlines, which are easy to confuse.

lines.text: Report a move within thirty days.

narration.text: Licenses arrive by mail only, never over DMV counters. If you move, you must tell DMV within thirty days, because the post office will not forward licenses and returns them instead. So licenses come only by mail, while address moves must reach DMV within thirty days since mail will not forward them. The two rules work together: because the license is mailed, DMV must have your current address to deliver it. The thirty-day deadline for reporting a move is the number to remember. A license mailed to an old address is returned instead of forwarded, which is why the thirty-day reporting rule matters.

lines.text: Title, registration, plates: within thirty days.
Plates front and rear with decals.

narration.text: Here is the trap. New residents often remember only one deadline. There are two. New Virginians owe a state license within sixty days, and title, registration and plates within thirty days. The plates go on the front and rear, with month and year decals in their plate slots, except on permanent plates. So newcomers owe licenses in sixty days but plates in thirty. The vehicle deadline comes first. If an exam question asks how long a new resident has to register a vehicle, the answer is thirty days. If it asks about the license, the answer is sixty. License sixty, plates thirty is the memory line for this pair of deadlines.

lines.text: Keep the card in the vehicle on every drive.
Register locally where your city or county demands it.

narration.text: Keep the registration card in the vehicle on every drive. And register locally too, where your city or county demands it. Put as a contrast: the card rides along on every drive, while locality registration applies only where cities or counties demand it. So the state registration card is a constant, carried every time you drive, while local registration depends on where you live. Together with the license you carry on your person, the registration card is part of the paperwork that travels with you. The next lessons add the yearly safety inspection and the insurance that registration requires.

lines.text: Plates on the front and rear.
Month and year decals in the plate slots.

narration.text: When a new resident registers a vehicle, the plates go on both the front and the rear of the vehicle. Month and year decals go in their slots on the plates, except on permanent plates, which do not carry them. All of this is due within thirty days of moving to Virginia, along with the title and registration. The license deadline is longer, sixty days. So the vehicle paperwork, the title, registration, plates and decals, comes first, and the license follows. Remember also that the registration card from this paperwork must ride in the vehicle on every drive.

Here is a quick check: Rosa has just moved to Virginia from another state. Which is due first, her Virginia license or her title, registration and plates? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the title, registration and plates, which are due within thirty days. The Virginia license is due within sixty days. Rosa puts the plates on the front and rear with their decals, keeps the registration card in the car on every drive, and registers locally if her city or county requires it. And when her license is issued, it will arrive by mail, so DMV needs her current address. License sixty, plates thirty.

lines.text: Licenses by mail; report moves in thirty days.

narration.text: To close the lesson: licenses arrive by mail only, never over DMV counters, and if you move you must tell DMV within thirty days, since the post office will not forward licenses. New Virginians owe a state license within sixty days, and title, registration and plates within thirty days, with plates front and rear and decals in their slots except on permanent plates. Keep the registration card in the vehicle on every drive, and register locally too where your city or county demands it. The memory line for new residents is: license sixty, plates thirty. The next lesson covers inspection and tires.

why_how.text: Every vehicle must pass a yearly safety inspection, with emissions testing in some localities.
Drivers check their own tires with the penny test and a pressure gauge.

scenario.text: Ben does the penny test, and the tread in the shallowest groove hides part of Lincoln's head.

reasoning.text: Tread hiding any of Lincoln's head means safe rubber, while less tread hurts wet grip.

result.text: Ben's tread passes, and he checks his tire pressures against the figure on the door jamb.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the yearly inspection is the only tire check a driver needs.

correction.text: The state inspects yearly with stickers, while drivers check tires monthly, starting with the penny pinch.

prompt.text: Ben's penny test shows the tread hiding part of Lincoln's head. Is the tread safe?

answer.text: Yes. Tread hiding any of the head means safe rubber.

rationale.text: Tread passes when it hides any of Lincoln's head, and pressure is checked against the manual or door jamb.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on inspection and tires. Virginia requires a yearly safety inspection, with a sticker to show it, and emissions testing in localities that order it. The manual also asks drivers to check their own tires, monthly or before a trip, using a simple test with a penny for tread and a gauge for pressure. By the end of this lesson you should know how often the state inspects, how to do the penny test from start to finish, and what to compare your tire pressure against. The penny test has two steps, starting the test and reading it, so we will go through each one in turn before the self-check.

lines.text: Pass the safety inspection every year.
Emissions testing where your locality orders it.

narration.text: Pass the yearly safety inspection, and display its sticker. Add emissions testing where your locality orders it. So the safety inspection applies to every vehicle every year, and emissions testing depends on where you live. Compare the driver's own checks: the state inspects yearly with stickers, while drivers inspect their tires monthly, starting with the penny pinch. The yearly inspection is a state requirement with a sticker as proof. The tire checks are something the manual asks you to do yourself, more often than once a year: monthly or before a trip.

lines.text: Pinch Lincoln's body between thumb and finger.
Sink Lincoln's head into the shallowest groove.

narration.text: Monthly, or before a trip, start the penny test by pinching Lincoln's body between your thumb and finger. Then sink Lincoln's head into the shallowest groove of the tread. If the tread hides any part of his head, the rubber is safe. If less of the head is covered, the tread is too thin, and wet grip suffers. So the test has two steps: hold the penny by Lincoln's body, and read how much of his head the tread covers. Use the shallowest groove for the reading, because that is where the manual tells you to place the penny. Tread passes when it hides any of Lincoln's head.

lines.text: Tread: hides any of Lincoln's head.
Compare with the owner's manual or door jamb.

narration.text: Here is the trap: the penny test checks tread, not tire pressure. Pressure is a separate check. Gauge your tire pressures before you get in, against the figure in the owner's manual or on the door jamb. So tread passes when it hides any of Lincoln's head, while pressure passes against the figure in the manual or on the door jamb. The manual asks for both checks: the penny for tread and the gauge for pressure. And note the source for the right pressure: it comes from the owner's manual or the door jamb, so you look it up for your own vehicle each time you check.

lines.text: Tread hides part of Lincoln's head.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ben does the penny test, and in the shallowest groove the tread hides part of Lincoln's head. Is his tread safe? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. Tread hiding any of Lincoln's head means safe rubber, while less tread hurts wet grip. Ben then checks his tire pressures with a gauge, against the figure in the owner's manual or on the door jamb, because the penny test does not measure pressure. He does these checks monthly or before a trip, separate from the yearly safety inspection. State yearly, you monthly.

lines.text: Penny for tread, gauge for pressure.

narration.text: To close the lesson: pass the yearly safety inspection and display its sticker, and get emissions testing where your locality orders it. Monthly or before a trip, start the penny test by pinching Lincoln's body between your thumb and finger, then sink Lincoln's head into the shallowest groove. Tread that hides any of his head means safe rubber, while less tread hurts wet grip. Gauge your tire pressures before you get in, against the figure in the owner's manual or on the door jamb. The memory line is: the state inspects yearly, and you check monthly. The next lesson covers the insurance that registration requires.

why_how.text: Registration requires liability insurance from a Virginia-authorized carrier or the uninsured-vehicle fee.
The fee buys no coverage, and driving uninsured without the fee brings a costly path back.

scenario.text: Tom registers his car and pays the five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee instead of buying insurance.

reasoning.text: The fee buys no coverage, only a one-year right to run the vehicle.

result.text: Tom may drive for the year, but he has no insurance coverage if he crashes.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the uninsured-vehicle fee is a kind of insurance.

correction.text: Liability insurance or the five hundred dollar fee buys registration, but only insurance buys coverage, while the fee buys a one-year pass.

memory_support.text: Fee is a pass, not a policy.

prompt.text: Tom paid the uninsured-vehicle fee. Is he covered if he crashes?

answer.text: No. The fee buys no coverage, only a one-year right to run.

rationale.text: Only insurance buys coverage; the fee buys a one-year pass to run the vehicle.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on insurance requirements. To register a vehicle in Virginia, you need liability insurance from a carrier authorized in Virginia, or you must pay a five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee. The manual sets minimum amounts of coverage, which changed on January one, two thousand twenty-two. It explains what the fee does and does not buy, what to do before dropping coverage, and what happens if you are caught driving with neither insurance nor the fee. By the end of this lesson you should know the minimums, the difference between the fee and coverage, and the path back after being caught uninsured.

lines.text: Before January two thousand twenty-two: twenty-five, fifty, twenty thousand.

narration.text: Registration requires liability insurance from a Virginia-authorized carrier, or the five hundred dollar uninsured fee. The minimums before January one, two thousand twenty-two were twenty-five thousand dollars per person, fifty thousand per crash and twenty thousand for property. After that date they are thirty thousand, sixty thousand and twenty thousand. The driving records of driving-age members of your household can affect your premiums. So pre-two thousand twenty-two policies floor at twenty-five, fifty and twenty, while post-two thousand twenty-two floors rise to thirty, sixty and twenty. Notice that the property minimum stayed the same while the other two rose.

lines.text: Only a one-year right to run.
Insure for the whole registration period.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Paying the five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee can feel like buying a kind of insurance. It is not. The fee buys no coverage, only a one-year right to run the vehicle. Insure across the whole registration period, even while the car is parked or not running, and surrender the plates and registration before dropping coverage. So liability insurance or the fee buys registration, but only insurance buys coverage, while the fee buys a one-year pass. A driver who pays the fee and then crashes has no coverage from the fee. The memory line is: the fee is a pass, not a policy.

lines.text: No insurance and no fee: driving privilege ends.
Six hundred dollar noncompliance payment or plan.
Insurer certificate for three years past reinstatement.

narration.text: If you are caught driving without insurance and without having paid the fee, your driving privilege ends until you make a six hundred dollar noncompliance payment, or set up a payment plan, and file an insurer certificate that must stay in place for three years past reinstatement. Compare the right way to stop insuring a vehicle: dropping coverage starts with surrendering the plates and registration, while getting caught uninsured starts a six hundred dollar payment and a three-year certificate. So there is a correct order for ending coverage, plates first, and a costly path back for drivers who skip it.

Here is a quick check: Tom registered his car by paying the five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee instead of buying insurance. If he crashes, is he covered? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. The fee buys no coverage, only a one-year right to run the vehicle. Only insurance buys coverage. If Tom later wants to stop insuring a car he has insured, he must surrender the plates and registration before dropping the coverage. And if he were caught with neither insurance nor the fee, he would face a six hundred dollar payment and a three-year insurer certificate. The fee is a pass, not a policy.

lines.text: Insurance or the five hundred dollar fee.
Minimums now thirty, sixty, twenty thousand.
Fee buys no coverage; surrender plates first.

narration.text: To close the lesson: registration requires liability insurance from a Virginia-authorized carrier, or the five hundred dollar uninsured fee. Minimums were twenty-five thousand per person, fifty thousand per crash and twenty thousand property before January one, two thousand twenty-two, and thirty thousand, sixty thousand and twenty thousand after. The fee buys no coverage, only a one-year right to run, so insure across the whole registration period, even parked, and surrender plates and registration before dropping coverage. Caught with neither, you face a six hundred dollar payment or plan plus an insurer certificate for three years past reinstatement.

why_how.text: DMV doubles as a voter registrar through the license form.
The same forms let you choose to be an organ, eye and tissue donor.

scenario.text: Mia, seventeen, checks yes for organ donation on her permit form.

reasoning.text: Decisions made at eighteen or older bind, while under-eighteen wishes yield to parents and guardians.

result.text: Mia's parents or guardians have the final say until she turns eighteen, and she tells her family her choice.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a seventeen-year-old's donor choice is binding.

correction.text: Donation decisions bind at eighteen, and below that age they yield to parents and guardians.

prompt.text: Mia, seventeen, checks yes for organ donation. Whose decision controls?

answer.text: Her parents or guardians, until she is eighteen.

rationale.text: Donation binds at eighteen and yields to parents below, while voting needs citizenship, residency and eighteen by election day.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on two choices you can make on DMV forms. DMV doubles as a voter registrar, so eligible applicants can register to vote through the license form. And the license, permit and ID forms let you choose to be an organ, eye and tissue donor. Each choice has an age rule and some conditions, and the two age rules both involve eighteen, which is why they are worth comparing side by side. By the end of this lesson you should know who can register to vote through DMV, who cannot without a court restoration, and whose decision controls a donor choice for someone under eighteen.

lines.text: Eighteen by the next general election.

narration.text: DMV doubles as a voter registrar through the license form. It serves citizens who reside in Virginia and who will be eighteen by the next general election. People with felony convictions, and people found legally incompetent, need their rights restored by a circuit court first. So voter registration through DMV needs three things: citizenship, Virginia residency, and being eighteen by the next general election. The age condition looks ahead to the election, so a person who is seventeen now but will be eighteen by the next general election can register. The court restoration rule applies to felons and to people found incompetent.

lines.text: Check yes to donate organs, eyes and tissue.
Eighteen or older: the decision binds.
Under eighteen: parents and guardians decide.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A seventeen-year-old checks yes for donation and assumes the choice is final. The manual says decisions made at eighteen or older bind, while the wishes of donors under eighteen yield to their parents and guardians. Every donor should also tell their family about the choice. So voting wants citizenship, residency and age eighteen by election day, while donation binds at eighteen and yields to parents below that age. Both rules involve eighteen, but they work differently: the voting rule looks ahead to the next election, and the donation rule depends on the donor's age when the decision is made.

lines.text: Every donor should tell their family.
The choice is made on license, permit or ID forms.

narration.text: To become a donor, check yes on your license, permit or ID form to donate organs, eyes and tissue. The manual adds that every donor should share the choice with their family. For donors eighteen or older, the decision binds. For donors under eighteen, the wishes yield to parents and guardians. So the manual asks every donor, adult or minor, to tell their family about the choice. Compare voter registration on the same form, which is open to citizens living in Virginia who will be eighteen by the next general election.

Here is a quick check: Mia is seventeen and checks yes for organ donation on her permit form. Whose decision controls? Work it out before reading on. The answer is her parents or guardians, until she is eighteen. Decisions made at eighteen or older bind, while under-eighteen wishes yield to parents and guardians. Mia should still tell her family about her choice, as every donor should. If Mia will be eighteen by the next general election, she can also register to vote on the license form, as a citizen residing in Virginia. Eighteen binds, and tell your family.

lines.text: Vote: citizen, resident, eighteen by the election.
Felons and the incompetent need court restoration.
Donation: binds at eighteen; tell your family.

narration.text: To close the section: DMV doubles as a voter registrar through the license form for citizens residing in Virginia who will be eighteen by the next general election, and people with felony convictions or found incompetent need circuit court restoration first. Check yes on a license, permit or ID form to donate organs, eyes and tissue. Decisions made at eighteen or older bind, while the wishes of donors under eighteen yield to parents and guardians, and every donor should share the choice with family. The memory line is: eighteen binds, and tell your family. This completes the Virginia manual's sections in this course.
